title: The longer ending (Mark 16:9–20)
hook: later verses add appearances and a commission; scholars note it wasn't in the earliest manuscripts

segments.voice: Yesterday, an empty tomb and women who fled in trembling and ekstasis. Your line was he goes before you.

Open a Bible to the end of Mark and you might notice something odd. After verse eight, many modern Bibles put in a line, a bracket, or a small note: some of the earliest manuscripts end here. Then they keep going. Twelve more verses. If yesterday's ending left you hanging, the women running and afraid, you're in good company. Very early on, Christians felt that too, and the church ended up with more than one way to finish the story.
screen: `A BRACKET AFTER VERSE EIGHT.` → `SOME MANUSCRIPTS END HERE.` → `TWELVE MORE VERSES.`

segments.voice: Here's what the longer ending says. The risen Jesus appears first to Mary Magdalene, out of whom he had cast seven devils. She tells the mourning disciples, and they don't believe her. He appears to two of them walking in the country; they tell the rest, and again nobody believes. Then he appears to the eleven at a meal and scolds them for their unbelief and hardness of heart. And he gives them their commission, in the King James Bible: "Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature." Then he is taken up into heaven, and they go out and preach everywhere. Now the honest part. The two oldest complete Greek manuscripts of Mark, from the three hundreds, stop at verse eight. These twelve verses differ from the rest of Mark in vocabulary and style, and they sound like a summary of appearances told in the other Gospels and Acts. So most scholars think a later hand added them. Some manuscripts even have a second, shorter ending, just a sentence or two. But the longer ending is also very old. A church writer named Irenaeus seems to quote it well before the year two hundred, and it's in the vast majority of manuscripts. Churches hold it in different ways. The Catholic and Orthodox churches receive it as part of scripture and read it in their services. Many Protestant Bibles print it with a note. Almost everyone agrees on what it's doing: finishing the thought. Fear becomes a mission. The disciples who fled are sent out into all the world.
screen: `MARY MAGDALENE, FIRST.` · `THEY DID NOT BELIEVE.` · `NOT IN THE OLDEST COPIES.` · `CHURCHES HOLD IT IN DIFFERENT WAYS.` · then, large: `GO YE INTO ALL THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: If you can, open Mark 16 and read verses one to eight slowly, then stop and notice how it feels to end on they were afraid. Then read verses nine to twenty and notice how it feels to end on a mission; you don't have to decide anything about manuscripts. If you pray, you can offer both, the fear and the going, to God.

Irenaeus, the early church writer who quotes Mark's longer ending well before the year two hundred. Appearances, a commission and an ascension, missing from the oldest copies and very old all the same.
Your line: go into all the world. Two endings: one afraid, one sent out. Day two hundred thirty, done.

fork.setup: you're one of the eleven. Mary Magdalene runs in and says she's seen him alive. what do you do, in the longer ending?
options: go to the tomb to check.
fork.reveal: they didn't believe her, or the two from the country either, until he appeared to them and scolded their unbelief.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mark has always had one ending.
what it means: the oldest copies end at 16:8; a longer ending (16:9–20) and a shorter one were added.
what a scholar hears: Sinaiticus and Vaticanus stop at 16:8, but Irenaeus seems to know the longer ending in the 100s.

sources.quoted: Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.

notes: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.10.5 (c. 180) quotes Mark 16:19; confirm reference and date.
Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (4th century) end at 16:8; confirm.

The Council of Trent affirmed the canonical books 'with all their parts'; Catholic reception of 16:9–20 as canonical is generally held. Orthodox read it in the Matins resurrection gospels. Confirm phrasing.
